title: Explore, plan, implement, commit: the Claude Code loop
titleVi: Khám phá, lập kế hoạch, triển khai, commit: vòng lặp làm việc với Claude Code

units.text: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
What you will be able to do
Run a Claude Code task as four separate phases (explore, plan, implement, commit) and say why research and planning come before any code is written
Choose the permission mode that matches how much the task should be allowed to change without your approval
Write prompts that point Claude at exact files, sources and symptoms instead of describing them loosely
Keep a session clean by interrupting, rewinding, clearing and delegating research to subagents
Give Claude a check it can run (a test, a screenshot or a build) so it can verify its own work
Key concept
Explore, plan, implement, commit

A Claude Code workflow that keeps reading and planning apart from editing. Claude first learns the relevant code, then proposes a plan you can review, and only after that writes, tests and commits the change.

Explore, plan, implement, commit

Claude Code is an agent. It reads files, runs shell commands, edits code and uses git in your project, so a vague request such as "add Google OAuth" can turn straight into edits across a codebase it has not read yet. The explore, plan, implement, commit loop prevents that. Each phase is its own prompt, and no code is written until Claude understands the existing code and you have agreed on a plan.
The four phases as separate prompts, using an OAuth feature as the example
text
Explore
asks Claude to read and explain, and nothing else.
Plan
asks which files will change and how the flow will work, and the answer is something you can review and correct while correcting it costs nothing.
Implement
refers back to "your plan" and includes its own check: write tests, run the suite, fix the failures.
Commit
turns the finished work into a commit and a pull request.
Plan mode makes the first two phases safe. If you start a session with

, Claude can investigate and propose changes but cannot write to your source files. You review the proposal and then leave plan mode to implement it, so nothing reaches disk until you have seen the plan.

Matching the permission mode to the task

The permission mode sets which actions Claude takes on its own and which ones wait for you. Choosing a mode is a workflow decision. Exploring an unfamiliar repo, reviewing untrusted code and doing a routine refactor each need a different amount of freedom.
Predict first
In Accept edits mode, Claude has finished editing three files and now wants to run
. What happens?
Claude asks you first, because Accept edits only auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands
The command is blocked outright, because Accept edits forbids shell commands
It runs without asking, because Accept edits approves everything Claude does

Long sessions where prompting on every step would slow you down

Take a security engineer reviewing a pull request from outside the team. Claude should read the files and run analysis, but every edit and every command needs the engineer's approval first. Manual is the only mode in the table that meets this. Accept edits would apply file changes without asking. Auto would let a classifier approve most actions. Plan blocks edits, but it is a mode for proposing changes, not for approving them one at a time. bypassPermissions goes further than any of these and drops the prompts entirely. It is not even in the normal Shift+Tab cycle until you start Claude Code with
. In recent versions of Claude Code, Auto is the built-in starting mode for interactive sessions, so you switch to Manual deliberately when you need it.
Between these modes, permission allowlists let you pre-approve individual commands you know are safe, such as
or
. Claude then stops asking about those commands while still asking about everything else. Pre-approving a few specific commands is safer than switching the whole session to a more permissive mode.
Exam trap
Accept edits mode still asks before every file edit, so it is a safe choice when someone must approve each change.
Why is that wrong?

Pointing Claude at exact context

The precision of a prompt limits the precision of the result. If you ask "fix the login bug", Claude has to search for the bug, guess what it is, and decide for itself when the fix is done. If you name the location, the scenario and the fix condition, it has none of those to guess. The table below pairs vague requests with specific versions of the same request.
Vague requests rewritten to give Claude the exact context
Technique
Vague
Specific
Scope the task
add tests for foo.py
write a test for foo.py covering the edge case where the user is logged out. avoid mocks.
Point to sources
why does ExecutionFactory have such a weird api?
look through ExecutionFactory's git history and summarize how its api came to be
Reference existing patterns
add a calendar widget
look at how existing widgets are implemented on the home page; HotDogWidget.php is a good example
Describe the symptom
fix the login bug
login fails after session timeout; check the auth flow in src/auth/, write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it
Referencing a file with
works better than describing where the code lives, because Claude reads the file before it responds.
puts that exact file in context. A directory reference such as
gives Claude the list of files in that directory, not their contents. Use it to orient Claude, then reference the files that matter.
Context can arrive in other ways too. You can paste or drag in a screenshot of an error or a design mockup. You can pipe data straight into Claude with
. You can give a documentation URL. Or you can tell Claude to fetch what it needs itself with Bash commands, MCP tools or file reads, which saves you from pasting large amounts of text.
Exam trap
Referencing a directory with @ loads the contents of every file in it into context.
Why is that wrong?

Redirecting, clearing and delegating

Correct a session as soon as it drifts. Waiting means more wasted work to undo. Press Esc to stop Claude in the middle of an action: the running tool call is cancelled and the context is kept, so you can redirect it straight away. If Claude is heading the right way and only needs a nudge, type the correction and press Enter without stopping it. The message is queued, and Claude reads it as soon as its current tool calls finish, within the same turn. If the work has already gone wrong, press Esc twice or run
to restore an earlier state of both the conversation and the code.
Leftover context also costs you. A long session full of material from an unrelated earlier task can make Claude perform worse. Run
between unrelated tasks to start from an empty context. For a quick side question, use
: its answer never enters the conversation history. When a session has to keep going,
summarizes it according to your instructions instead of whatever the automatic summary would choose to keep.

Subagents keep the main context clean in a different way. A prompt such as "use subagents to investigate how our authentication system handles token refresh" sends the file reading to a separate agent, and only its findings come back to your session. A subagent can also be a reusable specialist with a fixed tool set and its own instructions, defined in a file:
A subagent definition limited to read and search tools plus Bash, with its own model and instructions

Giving Claude a way to check its own work
Feedback loops and iterative refinement inside the system

mean the system checks its own output and improves on it. In Claude Code, that requires giving Claude something concrete to check against. "Implement a function that validates email addresses" has no finish line. Adding example cases (user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false) and the instruction "run the tests after implementing" gives Claude a result it can verify. UI work follows the same pattern: paste a screenshot of the design, ask Claude to screenshot its result, compare the two, and fix the differences. For a failing build, paste the actual error and ask for the root cause to be fixed, not for the error to be suppressed.
There are four ways to attach the check, depending on how long it needs to apply and how firmly it must hold:
In one prompt: ask Claude to run the check and keep iterating in the same message.
Across a session: set the check as a
condition. A separate evaluator re-checks it after every turn, and Claude keeps working until the goal is met.
As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes.
As a second opinion: a verification subagent has a fresh model try to refute the result, so the agent that did the work is not the one grading it.
Apply it to your own work
Think of the last change you asked an AI assistant to make. What check could it have run itself (a test, a build, a screenshot comparison) so that you did not have to be the one who verified it?
